title: Invasive Species and Food-Web Changes Review Test
description: Distinguish introduced species from harmful invaders, trace direct and indirect food-web effects, and evaluate evidence for management choices.

questions.prompt: A non-native garden plant remains confined and has no documented or likely harm in that setting. Which claim is justified from these facts?
questions.questionText: A non-native garden plant remains confined and has no documented or likely harm in that setting. Which claim is justified from these facts?
options: Every non-native plant must be invasive in every habitat.
Being attractive proves the plant cannot ever cause harm.
No further evidence could ever change its classification.
Non-native status alone does not establish that it is invasive there.
questions.correctAnswer: Non-native status alone does not establish that it is invasive there.
questions.explanation: Classification depends on context and impact evidence, not appearance or origin alone.

questions.prompt: A new grazing animal removes a native shrub used by insects. What indirect effect could reach insect-eating birds?
questions.questionText: A new grazing animal removes a native shrub used by insects. What indirect effect could reach insect-eating birds?
options: Birds receive more food because shrubs are fewer.
The animal directly consumes birds in this model.
All birds must immediately leave the region.
Reduced insect food may reduce food available to birds.
questions.correctAnswer: Reduced insect food may reduce food available to birds.
questions.explanation: A chain through host plants and insects connects the change to birds.

questions.prompt: A species appears in 12 of 60 equally sampled ponds. What share of the ponds contains it?
questions.questionText: A species appears in 12 of 60 equally sampled ponds. What share of the ponds contains it?
questions.explanation: 12 divided by 60 is 0.2, or 20%; this describes observed occupancy.

questions.prompt: Native plants decline near an introduced species and also near uninvaded dry sites. What should investigators consider?
questions.questionText: Native plants decline near an introduced species and also near uninvaded dry sites. What should investigators consider?
options: Only the introduced species can influence plants.
Dry sites provide no useful comparison.
Water shortage as an alternative or contributing cause.
Native decline proves the species eats plants.
questions.correctAnswer: Water shortage as an alternative or contributing cause.
questions.explanation: A similar decline elsewhere points to additional factors that need testing.

questions.prompt: Why can a dense introduced vine affect a tree without eating its leaves?
questions.questionText: Why can a dense introduced vine affect a tree without eating its leaves?
options: Only leaf-eating can harm a tree.
It may block light or otherwise change access to resources.
All vines supply trees with unlimited sugar.
Origin alone determines exactly how much light a tree receives.
questions.correctAnswer: It may block light or otherwise change access to resources.
questions.explanation: Competition and habitat modification can affect plants without predation.

questions.prompt: A food web shows algae -> small grazers -> fish. An introduced organism consumes much of the algae. Which prediction is plausible if algae become limiting?
questions.questionText: A food web shows algae -> small grazers -> fish. An introduced organism consumes much of the algae. Which prediction is plausible if algae become limiting?
options: Fish necessarily gain more energy immediately.
Small grazers may lose food, with possible later effects on fish.
Small grazers no longer need algae.
All algae matter becomes heat without passing through organisms.
questions.correctAnswer: Small grazers may lose food, with possible later effects on fish.
questions.explanation: A shared food reduction can propagate indirectly through feeding links.

questions.prompt: A native population falls from 75 to 48 individuals. How large is the decline?
questions.questionText: A native population falls from 75 to 48 individuals. How large is the decline?
options: 48 individuals.
75 individuals.
27 individuals.
123 individuals.
questions.explanation: The difference is 75 - 48 = 27; cause requires separate evidence.

questions.prompt: An invasive removal method also removes native ground cover and increases erosion. What should evaluation include?
questions.questionText: An invasive removal method also removes native ground cover and increases erosion. What should evaluation include?
options: Only the number of target plants removed.
Only how quickly workers finished.
Target reduction, native damage, and soil effects together.
Only whether the target's common name is correct.
questions.correctAnswer: Target reduction, native damage, and soil effects together.
questions.explanation: Effective management considers ecosystem outcomes and tradeoffs, not one target count.

questions.prompt: An introduced fish persists in one lake but fails in another. Which explanation is plausible?
questions.questionText: An introduced fish persists in one lake but fails in another. Which explanation is plausible?
options: Introduction guarantees identical outcomes.
Every lake provides the same resources.
Failure proves it was never introduced.
Different temperatures, resources, or interactions affect its success.
questions.correctAnswer: Different temperatures, resources, or interactions affect its success.
questions.explanation: Conditions and interactions vary across ecosystems.

questions.prompt: A treatment plot loses 40 target plants; an untreated matched plot loses 15 during a cold period. What is the difference in losses?
questions.questionText: A treatment plot loses 40 target plants; an untreated matched plot loses 15 during a cold period. What is the difference in losses?
options: 55 plants.
25 plants.
40 plants.
15 plants.
questions.explanation: 40 - 15 = 25; the reference helps account for shared change without proving every cause.

questions.prompt: Which evidence most helps test a proposed competition mechanism between native and introduced fish?
questions.questionText: Which evidence most helps test a proposed competition mechanism between native and introduced fish?
options: Both use the same limited food, and native growth improves when access by the introduced fish is reduced under matched conditions.
Both fish have scales.
Both names occur in a report.
The introduced fish was photographed first.
questions.correctAnswer: Both use the same limited food, and native growth improves when access by the introduced fish is reduced under matched conditions.
questions.explanation: A shared limiting resource plus a measured response tests competition more directly than co-occurrence.

questions.prompt: An introduced plant benefits one insect species but reduces several native host plants. Which conclusion is careful?
questions.questionText: An introduced plant benefits one insect species but reduces several native host plants. Which conclusion is careful?
options: Some organisms may benefit even when the overall ecological effect includes harm.
Any benefit means the plant cannot be invasive.
Every organism must respond identically.
Host-plant loss cannot affect other insects.
questions.correctAnswer: Some organisms may benefit even when the overall ecological effect includes harm.
questions.explanation: Mixed effects require looking across the community rather than choosing a single beneficiary.

questions.prompt: A control model assumes no new invaders enter a treated wetland. Boats continue arriving from infested waters. Which assumption needs review?
questions.questionText: A control model assumes no new invaders enter a treated wetland. Boats continue arriving from infested waters. Which assumption needs review?
options: Plants can no longer use light.
The site may receive new introductions across its boundary.
Native fish stop needing food.
The treatment date must change the laws of conservation.
questions.correctAnswer: The site may receive new introductions across its boundary.
questions.explanation: Continued transport can undermine a closed-site assumption and influence reinvasion.

questions.prompt: Invasive cover falls from 80% to 35%; native cover rises from 10% to 30%. Which comparison is correct?
questions.questionText: Invasive cover falls from 80% to 35%; native cover rises from 10% to 30%. Which comparison is correct?
options: Invasive cover fell 45 percentage points; native cover rose 20 percentage points.
Both changed by 45 percentage points.
Native cover rose 30 percentage points.
Invasive cover is now zero.
questions.correctAnswer: Invasive cover fell 45 percentage points; native cover rose 20 percentage points.
questions.explanation: Subtract initial and final values separately; neither target reduction nor native recovery is complete.

questions.prompt: One survey finds no target organisms after treatment. Which follow-up best checks lasting success?
questions.questionText: One survey finds no target organisms after treatment. Which follow-up best checks lasting success?
options: Assume permanent eradication from one survey.
Stop recording non-target effects.
Repeat standardized surveys over time and track native recovery and possible new arrivals.
Move surviving organisms to another habitat for comparison.
questions.correctAnswer: Repeat standardized surveys over time and track native recovery and possible new arrivals.
questions.explanation: Detection can be imperfect, and persistence, reinvasion, and ecosystem recovery require monitoring.
